title: Parameter-Decoupled Quantum Superresolution without Multiparameter Estimation
abstract: Quantum superresolution promises to resolve closely spaced sources beyond the diffraction limit, but existing approaches generally rely on idealized source properties or require simultaneous estimation of multiple coupled parameters of realistic sources. Here we introduce a parameter-decoupled measurement that determines the separation of realistic passive sources without estimating their unknown brightness imbalance, mutual coherence, or relative phase. A complete four-parameter quantum Fisher information analysis identifies the separation information that remains accessible in the presence of these nuisance parameters. We then construct a directly measurable log-probability invariant from projection channels whose conditional statistics depend only on the separation. Broad classes of channel pairs satisfy the resulting decoupling condition. For a Gaussian point-spread function, the lowest-order implementation asymptotically attains the four-parameter quantum limit per incident signal in the sub-Rayleigh regime. This approach converts a realistic multiparameter imaging problem into an operationally single-parameter measurement, providing a practical route toward quantum-enhanced resolution of passive spatial, temporal, and spectral signals.
summary: This paper introduces a novel measurement technique to achieve quantum superresolution for passive sources by eliminating the need to estimate unknown source parameters. By constructing a parameter-decoupled log-probability observable, the separation distance can be robustly determined, converting a complex multiparameter problem into a simple, single-parameter measurement.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of achieving quantum superresolution for closely spaced sources when the measurement is corrupted by unknown nuisance parameters (like brightness imbalance, coherence, or phase).
main_result: A parameter-decoupled measurement, based on a log-probability invariant, can be constructed that allows the separation distance to be determined without estimating these unknown nuisance parameters.
method: The authors use a complete four-parameter Quantum Fisher Information analysis to identify the accessible separation information, and then construct a measurement observable invariant under the nuisance parameters.
model_or_system: The system models a generic two-center signal from realistic passive sources, described by a mixed state dependent on separation ($s$) and nuisance parameters ($	heta = (s, b, g, \varphi)$).
key_observables: The directly measurable log-probability contrast, $D_{\alpha eta} = \ln p_\alpha - \ln p_ eta$, and the nuisance-adjusted Quantum Fisher Information, $F_{Q,s|\eta}$.
important_parameters: Separation distance ($s$), nuisance parameters ($b, g, \varphi$), and the sub-Rayleigh regime ($0 < s < \sigma$).
main_assumptions: The method relies on finding measurement channels that satisfy a specific parameter-decoupling condition ($R_\alpha(s) = R_ eta(s)$) and assumes a calibrated PSF.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the concept by showing how the log-probability observable $D_{\alpha eta}$ cancels common parameter dependence, leaving a function of $s$. Figure 3 confirms the finite information in the sub-Rayleigh regime.
paper_structure: The paper first analyzes the full four-parameter QFI, derives the parameter-decoupled observable $D_{\alpha eta}$ using specific measurement channels (like parity eigenmodes), and finally shows that the achievable classical Fisher information saturates the nuisance-adjusted quantum limit in the sub-Rayleigh regime.
why_interesting: This work provides a practical, resource-consistent method for quantum metrology in realistic, noisy environments, which is highly relevant for quantum optics and sensing applications.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Concept of parameter-decoupled quantum superresolution. (a) Two passive sources separated by s produce overlapping point-spread functions. Their brightness imbalance b, mutual-coherence magnitude g, and relative phase φ are generally unknown. (b) The received field is projected onto two “decoupled” channels, producing detection probabilities pα and pβ that depends on multiple source parameters b, g, φ. (c) Their log-probability observable Dαβ = ln pα −ln pβ = Dαβ(s) cancels the common dependence on b, g, and φ, leaving a function of the separation alone. The separation can therefore be recovered through ˆs = f(Dαβ) without estimating the three source-property nuisance parameters.

FIG. 2: General families of parameter-decoupled measurements. (a) For a pair of projection modes {ϕα, ϕβ}, the dependence on the source-property nuisance parameters cancels when their shifted-PSF overlap ratios satisfy Rα(s) = Rβ(s), where Rj(s) = ⟨ϕj|h+⟩/⟨ϕj|h−⟩. The general solutions turn into two families : parity eigenmodes and nonparity channels. For parity eigen modes, any two channels belonging to the same parity sector provide a parameter-decoupling solution. (b) Solution map for example pairs of Hermite–Gaussian modes (HGm, HGn).
